Chapter.Content: A rail, a wall, and a feasible region use the same nearest-point question
The rail projection minimizes distance to a line. We can ask the same question for a feasible set , the collection of states that satisfy the current constraints:

The notation requests a minimizing point, whereas requests the smallest objective value. For a nonempty closed convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, this point exists and is unique. “Closed” includes the set’s limit points. “Convex” means that the straight segment joining any two feasible points remains feasible.
Here is why uniqueness needs an argument. If two different points were equally nearest, convexity would make their midpoint feasible, while

would make it strictly nearer. A nonconvex set can have several equally nearest points: the center of a circle has every point on the circumference as a Euclidean nearest point. The circumference and the filled disk have different projection behavior.
At a nearest point , every feasible direction toward another point must initially fail to reduce distance. Differentiate along at to obtain

For a whole line or plane, feasible directions occur with both signs, so this becomes perpendicularity. At a corner or boundary, only an inequality remains. This explains why the old rail derivation is one case of a broader rule.
A halfspace is one side of a plane, , with nonzero normal . If is already inside, leave it alone. Otherwise
For , and , the projection is . The residual points outward. For every feasible , its dot product with is nonpositive, exactly as the optimality condition requires.

An axis-aligned box permits independent coordinate clamping under Euclidean distance. A slanted intersection of constraints generally does not. Repeatedly projecting onto each halfspace is an iterative algorithm, and one pass need not produce the nearest point in the intersection. An active constraint is one satisfied at equality at the solution; it helps identify which boundary currently matters.
If our error ruler is , the nearest point on the plane is instead

This follows by requiring the objective’s change to vanish along every feasible tangent direction. The correction follows , not generally the Euclidean normal . With and the same point and plane, , the multiplier is , and . It lies on the plane. Vertical error is expensive, so the solution changes the horizontal coordinate more strongly. Its squared -distance is , compared with for the Euclidean projection. The “closest” answer changes when the chosen cost changes.

Finally, the Euclidean residual provides a separating measurement when lies outside a closed convex set. Every point of the set is on one side of the supporting plane through ; a parallel plane midway between and strictly separates the point from the set. This connects projection to collision separation and constrained optimization without introducing a different mysterious mechanism.
This section develops the projection and separation treatment in Convex Optimization, physical PDF pages 411–414, using original rail/wall and weighted-distance examples.
A line fit is projection in observation space

Three measurements at times have values . Fit the model . Its possible predicted data vectors form the span of and in three-dimensional observation space. The closest prediction is therefore a projection onto that span, even though the fitted curve is a line in the original time-value plot.

Requiring residual to be perpendicular to both generating vectors gives and . Substitute the model to obtain and . Subtraction gives , then . The prediction is and residual is . Its ordinary sum and time-weighted sum are both zero. These are direct witnesses of least-squares optimality, not a promise that the linear model is scientifically correct.

MIT’s projection lesson emphasizes this connection between regression and linear projection. The numerical dataset here is an original example. The later matrix and QR chapters develop stable algorithms and rank-deficient cases. MIT OCW: Projection Matrices and Least Squares
Rotation first becomes understandable in a plane
Before constructing the panel’s three-dimensional frame, rotate its sensor sweep within a plane. Complex numbers provide a compact explanation.
Write a complex number as , where . Its real and imaginary components locate a point in a two-dimensional diagram. Addition adds these components. Multiplication follows distributivity:
Multiplication by sends to . Applying it twice sends the vector to , because . In conventional upward-positive Cartesian coordinates, one application is a counterclockwise quarter-turn.
For an arbitrary angle, use the unit complex number
Multiplying a coordinate pair by gives
For and , the result is . For , the same quarter-turn gives . Trigonometric functions in our code use radians: radians equal .
The conjugate of is . It satisfies
Therefore when . For a unit rotation, the inverse is just the conjugate. Multiplying two unit rotations composes them; angle-addition identities show that their angles add.

A non-unit multiplier rotates and scales, rather than only rotating. Repeated floating-point composition can gradually change the stored magnitude. Re-normalize under an explicit drift policy when the representation promises a rotation. The complex zero is not a valid rotation: multiplication by it collapses every point.

There is a numerical warning in the inverse formula. Squaring very large components can overflow even when a useful reciprocal exists; squaring tiny ones can underflow. Use a range-aware complex division algorithm rather than treating the displayed derivation as a universally safe implementation.

This excerpt implements multiplication, not a validated rotation type. The later laboratory uses a separate unit-vector wrapper for the same reason: a representation and a validated promise are different things.
Oriented area tells us which side of the panel is front
The panel needs a facing direction. Its edge vectors lie in its plane, so their dot product alone cannot provide an out-of-plane direction. We need oriented area.
The cross product and its definition

In an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean space, the cross product is perpendicular to both inputs. Its magnitude is the parallelogram area, and its sign follows the chosen orientation. Parallel inputs produce zero.
For a positively oriented orthonormal basis, the component rule is
This explicitly supplies the Part 542 definition absent as a standalone source. We now derive rather than merely memorize its components.
The signed area spanned by two coordinate pairs in the first two axes is the determinant

It is positive for the ordered pair of standard axes and changes sign when the arrows swap. Similar area measurements in the other coordinate planes give the three components above. The familiar symbolic determinant containing basis vectors is a mnemonic for these three signed minors, not a new unexplained arithmetic object.

Check perpendicularity directly: expand . Each product cancels a matching term of opposite sign, leaving zero. The same calculation with also gives zero. The construction is linear in each input and changes sign under exchange:
The panel’s normal and area
For the panel edges,
The raw result has magnitude , the parallelogram area. The triangular panel occupies half of that, so its area is . Its unit front normal is under this vertex ordering.
The identity

Image.alt: \|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\|^2 =\|\mathbf a\|^2\|\mathbf b\|^2-(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)^2
Image.originalTeX: \|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\|^2 =\|\mathbf a\|^2\|\mathbf b\|^2-(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)^2

Chapter.Content: follows by expanding both sides into products of components and cancelling matching terms. Insert the cosine relation to obtain
This is base times perpendicular height. It connects cross products, Gram determinants, area, and angle rather than introducing unrelated facts.

The cross components of nearly parallel inputs subtract nearly equal products. Their small result may be sensitive to rounding. The area identity is not automatically a numerically safer alternative: its right side can suffer severe cancellation too. Scale-aware nonparallelness is expressed by
with nonzero inputs and range-safe evaluation. A tiny raw cross magnitude alone may mean tiny geometry rather than nearly parallel directions.
Orientation is not storage order in memory
An ordered frame is right-handed relative to our chosen positive orientation when

It is left-handed when the sign is negative; zero means a degenerate frame, not a third handedness. Swapping two axes reverses the sign. Cyclic permutation preserves it. An orientation-preserving rotation cannot turn a right-handed frame into a left-handed one; a reflection can.
Handedness does not specify which axis is up, whether a camera looks toward positive or negative depth, or whether a matrix is stored by rows or columns. Define all these conventions separately.
For an orthogonal transform ,

A proper rotation has determinant . A reflection has determinant , so the oriented-area vector gains an extra sign. This explains why blindly treating a cross-derived normal as an ordinary direction through a mirror can reverse mesh orientation.

The same component cross formula encodes a chosen positive orientation. When using a basis of opposite orientation, decide whether the code’s algebraic convention or the external geometric orientation is authoritative and convert consistently. Calling a whole graphics API “left-handed” does not settle every stage of that pipeline.
Why three dimensions are special, but not the whole story
In two dimensions an oriented area has one independent component; it is not an in-plane perpendicular vector. The often-named “2D cross” is the scalar signed area .

In dimensions, oriented two-dimensional areas have independent components. In three dimensions that count equals three, allowing area components to be identified with a vector after a metric and orientation are chosen. In four dimensions there are six area components, not four. Also, two independent vectors in four-dimensional space have a two-dimensional perpendicular space rather than one uniquely oriented perpendicular direction.

There is an exceptional seven-dimensional binary cross product with additional structure. Do not turn the introductory three-dimensional explanation into the false claim that no such operation exists anywhere else. The ordinary graphics cross product remains the three-dimensional one described here.
Signed volume extends the same idea into space
Move a test point above the panel to . The scalar triple product is

Equivalently, dot the area normal with ; cyclic rearrangement preserves the scalar value. The signed parallelepiped volume is . The tetrahedron formed by four corners has one sixth of it, so its ordinary volume is .

Why area times height? The cross product contributes an area vector. Dotting with the third movement selects the signed component perpendicular to the base. A third vector lying in the base plane contributes zero height. Swapping two inputs reverses orientation, while taking absolute value gives ordinary volume.

In coordinates the triple product is a determinant. A determinant measures oriented area or volume scaling for a square linear map. A zero determinant indicates lost dimensions. It is not a universal conditioning score.
Nested cross products are not associative
The vector triple-product identity is

Image.alt: \mathbf a\times(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) =\mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c)-\mathbf c(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b).
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf a\times(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) =\mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c)-\mathbf c(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b).

Chapter.Content: For its first component, expand the left side:
Add the cancelling pair and recover the first component of the right side. The other components follow by cycling indices.
For the other grouping,

Image.alt: (\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)\times\mathbf c =\mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c)-\mathbf a(\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c).
Image.originalTeX: (\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)\times\mathbf c =\mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c)-\mathbf a(\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c).

Chapter.Content: These generally differ. Parentheses are part of the geometry, not optional punctuation. For example, , but .
For unit , the related identity

Image.alt: \mathbf n\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf n) =\mathbf v-\mathbf n(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n)
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf n\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf n) =\mathbf v-\mathbf n(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n)

Chapter.Content: is precisely tangent-plane rejection. A nested cross has now become a previously understood projection operation.
Immediate footing — derivative

A derivative is the best linear prediction of how a function changes near an input. For , , so near the leading change is and . The derivative is local: the omitted term matters for larger steps. Derivative units are output units divided by input units. At corners or discontinuities an ordinary derivative may not exist, so algorithms that rely on smoothness must state that assumption. Full explanation and worked examples in this book
A volume also constructs reciprocal measuring directions
In three dimensions, independent basis vectors have reciprocal directions

Image.alt: b^1=\frac{b_2\times b_3}{b_1\cdot(b_2\times b_3)},\quad b^2=\frac{b_3\times b_1}{b_1\cdot(b_2\times b_3)},\quad b^3=\frac{b_1\times b_2}{b_1\cdot(b_2\times b_3)}.
Image.originalTeX: b^1=\frac{b_2\times b_3}{b_1\cdot(b_2\times b_3)},\quad b^2=\frac{b_3\times b_1}{b_1\cdot(b_2\times b_3)},\quad b^3=\frac{b_1\times b_2}{b_1\cdot(b_2\times b_3)}.

Chapter.Content: The denominator is signed volume. A cross product measures oriented area; a scalar triple product measures oriented volume. These formulas explain the geometry, but a nearly collapsed volume makes reciprocal measurements sensitive to error. They are not a recommendation to use cross-product inversion for every floating-point basis solve. The cross product and signed volume just derived supply every operation in this construction.
An angle is a question with a domain
The unsigned angle between nonzero vectors lies in . The familiar expression is

After checking finite, nonzero inputs, clamp a small numerical overshoot of the computed cosine to . Clamping is not a substitute for valid inputs. Near parallel or antiparallel directions, the derivative of inverse cosine is large, so small cosine errors can produce relatively large angle errors.
Dot and cross provide cosine-like and sine-like information together. Therefore a useful alternative is

determines an angle from both components and their signs. Using the nonnegative cross length makes this an unsigned angle. Identical directions give zero; opposite directions give ; perpendicular directions give .

Scale each input by its own largest absolute component before computing dot and cross. Both quantities then acquire the same positive scale factor relative to the originals, leaving the angle unchanged while reducing overflow risk. This does not make cancellation disappear or recover already-rounded inputs.
A signed angle needs an orientation reference. For two vectors lying in a plane with unit positive normal ,
For arbitrary non-coplanar inputs, first define which plane or projected directions the signed angle refers to. A reference normal cannot resolve an unstated geometric question.
Often no angle is needed. To test whether unit directions differ by at most in , compare their dot product with . This saves inverse trigonometry and states the actual decision.
Surface movement becomes a local frame

The robot needs a front-facing normal and two directions along the panel. A tangent lies in a surface’s local tangent plane. A normal is perpendicular to that plane. A bitangent supplies a second tangent direction, often paired with increasing texture coordinates.

For a smooth parameterized surface , the partial derivatives and are local tangent vectors when they are independent. “Partial derivative” means the rate of change while varying one parameter and holding the other fixed. On a triangle, edge vectors directly span the flat tangent plane.
For a sphere centered at , the outward normal at a surface point follows . For a plane through with normal , points obey
A normal need not be unit length. If it is used as a signed distance ruler, it must be unit, otherwise the dot result contains an extra scale factor.

A geometric normal comes from the actual surface. A shading normal may be interpolated or modified to make lighting appear smooth. They can differ and have different responsibilities. Averaging unit normals usually yields a non-unit vector; re-normalize only after checking that the average has a usable direction. A collapsed triangle has no uniquely reliable face normal.
Texture coordinates specify preferred tangents

Let the panel corners have texture coordinates , , and . The panel’s position changes by when its first texture parameter increases by one, and by when the second increases by one. The raw texture tangents therefore carry spatial stretch, not merely direction.
For general texture differences, write

Image.alt: \mathbf e_1=\Delta u_1\mathbf t+\Delta v_1\mathbf b, \qquad \mathbf e_2=\Delta u_2\mathbf t+\Delta v_2\mathbf b.
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf e_1=\Delta u_1\mathbf t+\Delta v_1\mathbf b, \qquad \mathbf e_2=\Delta u_2\mathbf t+\Delta v_2\mathbf b.

Chapter.Content: Eliminate one unknown at a time. With
the result is

Image.alt: \mathbf t=\frac{\Delta v_2\mathbf e_1-\Delta v_1\mathbf e_2}{D}, \qquad \mathbf b=\frac{\Delta u_1\mathbf e_2-\Delta u_2\mathbf e_1}{D}.
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf t=\frac{\Delta v_2\mathbf e_1-\Delta v_1\mathbf e_2}{D}, \qquad \mathbf b=\frac{\Delta u_1\mathbf e_2-\Delta u_2\mathbf e_1}{D}.

Chapter.Content: is the signed texture-area scale. Zero means the texture triangle has collapsed and cannot identify two distinct texture directions. Nearly zero can amplify input error. Spatial degeneracy and texture degeneracy are separate checks.
Clean the frame without erasing its orientation
Given a unit normal and raw tangent , remove normal contamination and normalize:

Image.alt: \mathbf t'=\mathbf t-(\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n, \qquad \widehat{\mathbf t}=\operatorname{normalize}(\mathbf t').
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf t'=\mathbf t-(\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n, \qquad \widehat{\mathbf t}=\operatorname{normalize}(\mathbf t').

Chapter.Content: To preserve a mirrored texture island, keep a handedness sign

Image.alt: h=\operatorname{sign}\big((\mathbf n\times\widehat{\mathbf t})\cdot\mathbf b_{\mathrm{raw}}\big), \qquad \widehat{\mathbf b}=h(\mathbf n\times\widehat{\mathbf t}).
Image.originalTeX: h=\operatorname{sign}\big((\mathbf n\times\widehat{\mathbf t})\cdot\mathbf b_{\mathrm{raw}}\big), \qquad \widehat{\mathbf b}=h(\mathbf n\times\widehat{\mathbf t}).

Chapter.Content: When the sign test is zero or too uncertain, the input frame does not reliably determine handedness. Do not quietly invent a positive sign while claiming the original frame was valid.

The resulting TBN frame consists of tangent, bitangent, and normal. It converts a texture-local normal into the surface’s frame through weighted column addition. Document whether is encoded with this convention or its opposite.

The distinction between geometric and shading frames is used in real rendering systems; PBRT’s triangle implementation separately constructs these quantities and accounts for orientation reversal. That reference is an implementation anchor, not evidence that our simplified lab covers every seam and interpolation rule. PBRT, Triangle Meshes.
Immediate footing — rank and nullspace

The rank of a map is the number of independent output directions it can produce. Its nullspace (kernel) contains inputs mapped to zero. For , only one output direction is independent, so ; every vector lies in the nullspace. Rank plus nullity equals the input dimension: . In solving , rank shows which constraints are independent and which input directions remain free. In floating-point work, numerical rank uses a tolerance because an exact zero may appear as a small computed singular value.

Chapter.Content: Orthonormal frames make reconstruction simple
A frame is orthonormal when all its axes have length one and are mutually perpendicular. Its Gram matrix is identity. Coordinates of a vector are simply its dot products with the axes:
Orthonormality is why local lighting directions can be measured without solving a slanted-basis system each time.
Build a frame from one direction
A unit normal does not uniquely specify two tangent axes: they may rotate around it. We must choose a convention.
Choose a coordinate axis least aligned with the normal. In practice, select the axis corresponding to the smallest absolute component of . Then compute

Image.alt: \mathbf t=\operatorname{normalize}(\mathbf h\times\mathbf n), \qquad \mathbf b=\mathbf n\times\mathbf t.
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf t=\operatorname{normalize}(\mathbf h\times\mathbf n), \qquad \mathbf b=\mathbf n\times\mathbf t.

Chapter.Content: Because one squared component of a unit normal is at most , this helper has

So this exact-arithmetic helper cannot become almost parallel to the normal. For and helper , tangent is and bitangent . These are valid axes even though they differ from a texture-preferred orientation.

This construction is easy to teach, but its selected helper can change abruptly at tie boundaries. That matters for animated or spatially coherent frames. Robustness against division by a small quantity does not guarantee continuity of the output convention.

Research on orthonormal-basis construction investigates such numerical behavior. Duff and colleagues’ Building an Orthonormal Basis, Revisited is a useful comparison target for a faster specialized construction. We use the transparent helper-axis method here; we do not claim to have benchmarked or implemented that paper’s algorithm. Duff et al., 2017.
Gram–Schmidt is repeated rejection
Given independent generators , first normalize to . Then remove its component from the second generator:

Image.alt: \mathbf u_2=\mathbf v_2-(\mathbf v_2\cdot\mathbf q_1)\mathbf q_1, \qquad \mathbf q_2=\mathbf u_2/\|\mathbf u_2\|.
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf u_2=\mathbf v_2-(\mathbf v_2\cdot\mathbf q_1)\mathbf q_1, \qquad \mathbf q_2=\mathbf u_2/\|\mathbf u_2\|.

Chapter.Content: For the third,

Image.alt: \mathbf u_3=\mathbf v_3 -(\mathbf v_3\cdot\mathbf q_1)\mathbf q_1 -(\mathbf v_3\cdot\mathbf q_2)\mathbf q_2, \qquad \mathbf q_3=\mathbf u_3/\|\mathbf u_3\|.
Image.originalTeX: \mathbf u_3=\mathbf v_3 -(\mathbf v_3\cdot\mathbf q_1)\mathbf q_1 -(\mathbf v_3\cdot\mathbf q_2)\mathbf q_2, \qquad \mathbf q_3=\mathbf u_3/\|\mathbf u_3\|.

Chapter.Content: Each new axis keeps only movement not represented by previous axes. Because we subtract combinations of earlier generators, the span is preserved. A zero residual reveals dependence. A very small residual may reveal near dependence and unreliable input geometry.
Use and . The first axis is . The projection of the second is . The residual is , yielding axis . Both original generators remain in the reconstructed span.
Modified order changes floating-point behavior

Classical Gram–Schmidt evaluates every projection coefficient against the original current generator, then subtracts the combined projections. Modified Gram–Schmidt repeatedly measures and subtracts from the updated residual:
Chapter.Code: r = current generator for each earlier unit axis q: coefficient = dot(q, r) r = r - coefficient * q validate the residual, then normalize it
Chapter.Content: They agree in exact arithmetic when previous axes are exactly orthonormal. Floating-point axes and subtractions are not exact, so the order matters. Modified Gram–Schmidt often retains orthogonality better, but it cannot repair fundamentally uncertain near-dependent inputs. A second orthogonalization pass can help; rank detection and tolerance remain deliberate policies.
Validate both and under declared norms. The first checks axis orthogonality; the second checks reconstruction. A small reconstruction error alone does not prove good orthogonality.

For dense general-purpose solves, Householder QR is an important alternative. LAPACK represents the orthogonal factor through elementary reflectors rather than simply materializing a Gram matrix. This is the next-depth connection, not a new dependency for this vault’s small laboratory. LAPACK, QR Factorization.
